doc.title: Pete Candoli interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 15, 1999

title: Hearing Lunceford and Chick Webb; hotel bands and their signature sounds
summary: Pete recalls his music teacher's indifference, Chick Webb's 'Jitney Man' and how hotel bands each had a distinctive product sound.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Your ear must have been getting some really good training between the off-beats on the peck horn and the string bass.

Yeah it was quite amazing. I remember coming into the eighth grade and I had a little 78 of “Patricia,” and I’m trying to tell the music teacher, like we’d always march in the classrooms on Haydn [scats]. But I was really amazed. I said, “Don’t you hear what’s happening?” I would tell her, “Can’t you hear these sounds?” I mean it killed me then. I was in the eighth grade. And so, “Well yes, that’s very nice, Walter,” that’s my real name is Walter, see? And I said okay. It didn’t give her a charge. And I just got a bigger charge when I heard my first Jimmy Lunceford record sound. And “Jitney Man” by — somebody on piano voted for me for the Esquire magazine award, which I was elected one year, and I can’t think of his name.
No, no, he wasn’t with Jimmy Lunceford. He recorded a thing called the “Jitney Man” with a big band. He’s a drummer originally. I’ll think of it somewhere down the line.

Chick Webb. Isn’t that amazing? I remember him and that, and I say — because very few people even knew who Chick Webb was, let alone get on the record. It was usually hotel bands, and a few oddballs that were playing for listeners. And then it dawned upon me all the hotel bands had a pattern, a sound. It was like a product. They were smart. Like Sammy Kaye had [scats] before the singer got up, and Horace Hite [scats] all the triple tonguing. And everybody had a thing. Tommy Dorsey even played the first sixteen of a ballad, a solo tone mute with clarinets in the background, the first sixteen.
I see. So that they had a signature that you would recognize.
Oh yeah, Guy Lombardo, you knew every time you put the needle down it was Guy Lombardo. It was amazing.
So that’s the kind of bringing up—
